Course

Elevation profile

Height along the route and between checkpoints.

Elevation profile

What it shows

Height along the route, with the biggest climbs and descents numbered. Under the graph, for each section between checkpoints: its length and how much it climbs and descends. Checkpoints: CP1 Val Travenanzes, CP2 Col Gallina, CP3 Passo Giau, CP4 Rifugio Croda da Lago, CP5 Mortisa.

How to read it

Orange figures are climb, blue figures descent. Point at a leg to trace it on the map. A numbered climb or descent also highlights its table row. Select to pin.

Keep in mind

The profile and legs use the GPX track. Heights are smoothed over 60 m, so totals can differ from the published course figures. Checkpoint positions come from the organiser’s list, not from GPS.

Sources and method

In the page footer: Route and elevation.

Pace by leg

What it shows

Each runner’s leg pace is divided by their whole-race pace. The chart averages these ratios across runners with complete checkpoint times. 1.10× means 10% slower.

How to read it

Bar colours: teal below 0.90×, cream 0.90–1.10×, sand 1.10–1.25×, orange 1.25× or more. The printed factor is the exact value.

Keep in mind

This is pace, not effort: stops count, and it resolves only between checkpoints.

Timing coverage

1,347 of 1,372 finishers had complete checkpoint times in 2026.

Climbs and descents

The biggest swings in height, in course order.

Climbs and descents

What it shows

The 3 biggest climbs and 2 biggest descents in course order: length, height gained or lost, and the steepest 500 m.

How to read it

Numbers match the profile. A 10% grade is 10 m of height per 100 m. The steepest 500 m is its steepest average grade over any stretch of that length.

Keep in mind

A climb or descent is a change of at least 30 m between a peak and the next valley. Smaller ups and downs show only in the profile.

Finish times by year

Elapsed time from start to finish.

Finish times by year

What it shows

For each edition: the middle finisher (white tick) and the middle 80% of finishers (solid bar). The pale bar runs from the fastest to the slowest finisher.

How to read it

The middle finisher is the median: half finished faster, half slower. Choosing a finish position marks that group on every bar.

Keep in mind

Only classified finishers count. The did-not-finish share is the percentage of all timing records without a classified finish. The records can include non-starters.

Years covered

The recorded timing routes closely align across all three editions.

Against similar races

What it shows

Finish times in hours. 184 races within ±5% of this course’s distance and climb (50 km, 2,600 m). Each needs at least 100 participants. Other courses at this event are excluded.

How to read it

Pale bar: full range (nearly all for similar races). Solid bar: middle 80%. White tick: median.

Keep in mind

Terrain and conditions can differ. Races with full results: 109 for all finishers, 83 for women, 109 for men. Matches use year, name, distance, field size and average finish time.

Finish times

Estimated finish windows by rank, counted from the race start.

Finish times

What it shows

Five finish-rank groups, from the fastest to the last finisher. Their clock times are estimated by adding historical finish durations to the reference start time.

How to read it

The thin line marks the start or first wave. Cream shows daylight and slate shows the hours between sunset and sunrise. Select a rank to highlight its finish window.

Keep in mind

Sunrise and sunset at the start location are approximate. Mountain shadow, weather and tree cover can change when the course feels dark.

Weather

By year

Weather estimates near the start and at the course high point, 08:00–20:00 local time on each race day.

By year

What it shows

Air and feels-like ranges, peak gust and highest rain total across the reference sites. Feels-like estimates account for wind, humidity and sunlight. The last row shows the range across editions.

How to read it

Both bars use the same scale, from low (blue) to high (orange). Raindrops are solid from 5 mm, pale from 1 mm and outlined below that.

Keep in mind

Modeled values for the reference sites, not measured along the course. The model grid is about 25 km.

Where the data comes from

Trailguide is independent of the race organiser and data providers. Historical data may contain errors or gaps. Check the linked sources before relying on a figure. For the current route, cut-offs and rules, see the official race website.

Course

Route and elevation

Distance and climb in the header and comparisons come from the organiser’s 2026 figures. The profile and legs follow the timing provider’s route with heights from Copernicus GLO-30. Elevation is smoothed, so climb totals can differ. Checkpoint distances come from the timing provider’s list.

Climb comparison

Climb figures come from Maarten Poirot’s UTMB Index dataset. Each course of similar distance counts once, using its latest qualifying year.

Terrain picture

Terrain heights come from Copernicus GLO-30. The red line follows the course track. Use the official course map for navigation. ESA WorldCover 2021 identifies built-up areas in brown and water in blue.

Time

Finish times

Published results · 2026 LiveTrail, 2025 LiveTrail, 2024 LiveTrail

Pace by leg

The 2026 LiveTrail checkpoint times give each runner’s pace per leg. It is compared with their whole-race pace, including stops.

Similar races

Races are matched by distance and climb using Maarten Poirot’s UTMB Index dataset (2017–2024). The bars use matched results from DUV. Each race counts equally.

Start and daylight

Finish windows combine past finish times with the recorded start. Sunrise and sunset are estimates for the start location. Mountain shade can make parts of the route dark earlier.

Weather

Race-day estimates

Air and feels-like temperatures, rain and gusts come from hourly ERA5 estimates via Open-Meteo. The estimates cover sites near the start and at the course high point. Conditions can vary elsewhere on the course.
